rows.name: Quinn Chapel AME Church
rows.evidence_note: Chicago's oldest Black congregation; founded 1847. Continuous operation per sibling CTL-DR-SCI-004 research; confirm current service schedule via congregation site before public use.

rows.name: Olivet Baptist Church
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1853; historically one of the largest Black Baptist congregations in the U.S. Operating status per general and sibling sources.

rows.name: Bethel AME Church
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1862. Operating status per sibling CTL-DR-SCI-004 research.

rows.name: Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1902 (4501 S. Vincennes). Operating status per general knowledge; confirm before public use.

rows.name: Pilgrim Baptist Church (congregation)
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1922; birthplace of gospel music (Thomas A. Dorsey). Historic sanctuary destroyed by roof-repair fire in January 2006; surviving walls remain and a National Museum of Gospel Music is planned for the site, but the congregation worships elsewhere and the original worship/performance/archive environment was not rebuilt (Religion News Service 2006; GRAMMY.com).

rows.name: First Church of Deliverance
rows.evidence_note: Founded May 8, 1929 by Rev. Clarence H. Cobbs; landmark 1939 building at 4315 S. Wabash by Walter T. Bailey (Chicago Landmark, 1994). Pioneering radio ministry (WSBC, 1935) and first Black church to televise services (WLS-TV, 1953); Cobbs later headed the Metropolitan Spiritual Churches of Christ (130 churches). Still operating: the church’s own listings show Sunday services in 2026 (findglocal). (Wikipedia; church listings.)

rows.name: Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1950 by Rev. Clay Evans. Operating.

rows.name: Liberty Baptist Church
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1915 (4849 S. King Drive). Operating status per general knowledge; confirm before public use.

rows.name: Trinity United Church of Christ
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1961; led by Rev. Jeremiah Wright 1972-2008. Operating megachurch.

rows.name: Mosque Maryam (Nation of Islam National Center)
rows.evidence_note: Nation of Islam national headquarters mosque. Operating.

rows.name: Chicago Conservator
rows.evidence_note: Ferdinand L. Barnett's paper; Chicago's first Black newspaper (1878-1914) per Illinois Black-newspaper list.

rows.name: Chicago Defender
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1905 by Robert S. Abbott. Sold out of Sengstacke family ownership to Real Times investors 2003; daily-to-weekly conversion; print ended 2019 for digital focus. Circulation fell from ~230,000 peak weekly sales to 14,629 daily sales in 2002 (Editor & Publisher). Title and online editorial presence survive; daily print frequency and physical distribution ended.

rows.name: Chicago Bee
rows.evidence_note: Anthony Overton's paper, cross-subsidized within his bank/cosmetics/building ecosystem. Continued briefly under his sons after his death; closed 1947. Very little of its run survives — an archival-function loss (Wikipedia). Founding year commonly cited as 1925; verify via Bee Building landmark report.

rows.name: Chicago Whip
rows.evidence_note: Founded June 24, 1919 by William C. Linton; financed by Anthony Overton, Jesse Binga, and Oscar De Priest. Its 'Don't Spend Money Where You Can't Work' campaign led to 15,000+ Chicago Blacks securing jobs. Ceased publication 1939 (Wikipedia; NEH).

rows.name: Chicago Crusader
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1940 by Balm L. Leavell and Joseph H. Jefferson (as The Crusader / The New Crusader). Published by Balm Leavell until his death in 1968, then by widow Dorothy Leavell. Chicago's longest-running African-American weekly; still publishing (Wikipedia; NNPA member listing).

rows.name: Chicago Citizen (Citizen Newspaper Group)
rows.evidence_note: Weekly; NNPA member (Hyde Park and South Suburban listings). Still publishing.

rows.name: N'Digo
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1989 by Hermene Hartman (commonly cited). Current publishing status not confirmed in this track's sources — marked unknown rather than guessed.

rows.name: The Final Call
rows.evidence_note: Official newspaper of the Nation of Islam; twice-monthly; still publishing per Illinois Black-newspaper list.

rows.name: Chicago Standard News
rows.evidence_note: Weekly; listed as current in the Illinois African-American newspapers list.

rows.name: Negro Digest / Black World
rows.evidence_note: Johnson Publishing's digest (1942); renamed Black World 1970; closed 1976.

rows.name: Ebony
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1945 by John H. Johnson. Sold to Clear View Group (private equity) 2016; Johnson Publishing filed Chapter 7 in 2019; brand later passed to Junior Bridgeman's Ebony Media (2020/21). Magazine brand survives but the Chicago publishing operation and Black family ownership ended — a fragmentation case (CJR; NPR Illinois).

rows.name: Jet
rows.evidence_note: Left print in 2014; digital-only thereafter; ceased with ownership turmoil and Johnson Publishing bankruptcy (CJR). Print institution closed.

rows.name: Johnson Publishing Company
rows.neighborhood: South Loop (820 S. Michigan, former HQ)
rows.evidence_note: Sold Ebony/Jet to Clear View Group 2016; filed Chapter 7 bankruptcy 2019 (NPR Illinois; CJR). Headquarters building and photo archive passed to separate custodians.

rows.name: Third World Press
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1967 by Haki Madhubuti; one of the largest Black-owned independent presses. Operating status per general knowledge; direct institutional confirmation recommended.

rows.name: Jack L. Cooper radio programming (WSBC)
rows.evidence_note: Cooper is widely cited as Chicago's first Black radio announcer (WSBC, 1929). Program/institution end date and any direct successor not established in this track's sources — marked unknown.

rows.name: WVON 1690 AM
rows.evidence_note: Call letters established 1963 under Chess ownership; later owned by Globetrotter Communications and Gannett; current Black-owned operator Midway Broadcasting recovered the call letters. Operating with leased frequency infrastructure (Congressional Record, Vol. 159).

rows.name: WGCI-FM 107.5
rows.evidence_note: Black-format urban station (as WGCI from 1974); not Black-owned (iHeartMedia). Included to distinguish Black-format from Black-owned radio. Operating.

rows.name: WVAZ-FM 102.7 (V103)
rows.evidence_note: Urban adult-contemporary format from 1978; not Black-owned. Operating.

rows.name: Binga State Bank
rows.evidence_note: Founded by Jesse Binga; closed 1930. Binga was convicted in 1933, maintained innocence, and received a full pardon in 1941 — treat cause/responsibility as potentially disputed, not a simple fraud narrative (BlackPast).

rows.name: Douglass National Bank
rows.evidence_note: Second Black-owned national bank; closed 1932 in the Depression. Dates commonly cited; verify via OCC/FDIC records before public use.

rows.name: Illinois Service Federal Savings and Loan
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1934 by 13 Black men during the Great Migration. Acquired by Ghanaian-owned Groupe Nduom April 2016; renamed GN Bank effective July 2018 (OCC CRA evaluations). The Black-American-owned charter ended; the banking operation continued under new ownership and name.

rows.name: GN Bank (successor to Illinois Service Federal)
rows.evidence_note: Renamed from Illinois Service Federal July 2018 under Groupe Nduom ownership; Ghanaian-owned CDFI serving South Side. OCC terminated its consent order June 30, 2025, declaring it safe and sound (TodayGH). Chatham branch closed 2020 (OCC 2023 CRA eval).

rows.name: Seaway National Bank
rows.evidence_note: Closed by regulators January 2017. State Bank of Texas assumed deposits and bought assets; $240M in deposits and nine branches sold to Self-Help Federal Credit Union; State Bank retained the O'Hare branch and ~$200M loan portfolio (Banking Exchange). Depositor access survived; the locally Black-owned bank and unified local deposit-to-loan allocation did not.

rows.name: Independence Bank of Chicago
rows.evidence_note: Black-owned bank founded 1968; failed 1995. Commonly cited dates; verify via FDIC records before public use.

rows.name: ShoreBank (South Shore Bank)
rows.evidence_note: Community-development bank closed by FDIC August 20, 2010; Urban Partnership Bank acquired deposits and branches (FDIC Failed Bank List).

rows.name: Urban Partnership Bank
rows.evidence_note: CDFI successor to ShoreBank (est. Aug 20, 2010). Merged into Providence Bank & Trust January 2019; Providence lacked Urban Partnership's intensive community-development focus (FDIC; Next City).

rows.name: Self-Help Federal Credit Union (former Seaway branches)
rows.evidence_note: Durham, NC-based CDFI credit union; acquired nine former Seaway branches and $240M in deposits in 2017 (Banking Exchange). Mission-aligned successor but not Black-owned. Operating.

rows.name: Supreme Life Insurance Company
rows.evidence_note: First northern Black-owned insurance company (per IIT); Supreme Life Building is a Black Metropolis Chicago Landmark (1998). Taken over by the Illinois Department of Insurance in 1999 due to insolvency and placed into rehabilitation. Takeover sourced to a weak secondary (answers.com) — grade Provisional and seek Tribune/DOI primary before public use.

rows.name: Provident Hospital (original Black-owned)
rows.evidence_note: First Black-owned and operated hospital in the U.S. with a Black nursing school. Private hospital closed 1987; Cook County purchased it in 1991, invested over $50M, and reopened it in 1993 as a public community teaching hospital (Cook County Health FAQ). Healthcare service was restored; independent Black ownership/control and the original race-specific professional-training function were not restored in the same form.

rows.name: Provident Hospital of Cook County
rows.evidence_note: Public successor to Provident Hospital; purchased by Cook County 1991, reopened 1993. Operating.

rows.name: Wendell Phillips Academy High School
rows.evidence_note: CPS high school; first Chicago high school attended predominantly by Black students. Operating.

rows.name: DuSable High School (original comprehensive)
rows.evidence_note: Opened February 1935 (built 1931-34, architect Paul Gerhardt Sr.). Reconstituted under CPS Renaissance 2010 into smaller academies in the same building from 2005; building designated a Chicago Landmark May 1, 2013 (Wikipedia; a-better-place.com). The unified comprehensive high school ended; the building continues in educational use.

rows.name: Bronzeville Scholastic Institute
rows.evidence_note: Small CPS school created in the 2005 DuSable split; still operating in the landmark building (enrollment ~114 in 2025-26 per Wikipedia).

rows.name: Daniel Hale Williams Preparatory School of Medicine
rows.evidence_note: Small CPS school created in the 2005 DuSable split; still operating (enrollment ~82 in 2025-26 per Wikipedia).

rows.name: Walter H. Dyett High School (original)
rows.evidence_note: CPS closed Dyett in 2015 over community opposition (Chicago Reporter; KOCO).

rows.name: Dyett High School for the Arts
rows.evidence_note: Reopened 2016 after a 34-day hunger strike — but under CPS control and not the community-demanded curriculum (Chicago Reporter; KOCO). Succession preserved a neighborhood high school; community governance was not restored.

rows.name: Chicago Military Academy-Bronzeville
rows.evidence_note: CPS military academy opened 1999 in the renovated Eighth Regiment Armory after National Trust-recognized restoration (Wikipedia). Operating.

rows.name: Chicago State University
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1867 as Cook County Normal School; predominantly Black public university on the South Side. Operating.

rows.name: Kennedy-King College
rows.evidence_note: City Colleges of Chicago; originated as Woodrow Wilson Junior College (1935), renamed for Robert F. Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr. in 1969. Dates commonly cited; verify before public use. Operating.

rows.name: Olive-Harvey College
rows.evidence_note: City Colleges of Chicago, founded 1970. Operating.

rows.name: Malcolm X College
rows.evidence_note: City Colleges of Chicago; originated as Crane Junior College (1911), renamed for Malcolm X in 1969. Operating.

rows.name: Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection
rows.evidence_note: Chicago Public Library's Black history and literature collection; founded 1932 by Chicago's first Black librarian, Vivian Harsh. Operating.

rows.name: DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1961 by Margaret Taylor-Burroughs and colleagues as the Ebony Museum of Negro History and Art; renamed for Jean Baptiste Point DuSable; moved to Washington Park Burnham building 1973. Renamed 'DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center' at a Juneteenth 2022 unveiling (WTTW/Chicago Tonight). Smithsonian affiliate. Operating.

rows.name: South Side Community Art Center
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1940; oldest continuously operating Black art center in the U.S. Chicago Landmark designation commonly cited as 2024 — verify before public use. Operating.

rows.name: Bronzeville-Black Metropolis National Heritage Area
rows.evidence_note: Established by the National Heritage Area Act (Public Law 117-339), passed by Congress December 2022 and signed January 5, 2023; up to $10M over 15 years; coordinated by the Bronzeville-Black Metropolis National Heritage Area Commission under Paula Robinson (Sun-Times via Ebony4Alderman; IIT). Operating.

rows.name: A. Philip Randolph Pullman Porter Museum
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1995; honors Black railroad labor history. Operating status per general knowledge; confirm before public use.

rows.name: Bronzeville Children's Museum
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1999; only Black children's museum in the country (commonly cited). Operating status per general knowledge; confirm before public use.

rows.name: National Museum of Gospel Music (planned)
rows.evidence_note: Planned/developing on the Pilgrim Baptist Church site after the 2006 fire (GRAMMY.com). Not yet opened as of this track's research; marked unknown rather than operating.

rows.name: Pekin Theatre
rows.evidence_note: Robert T. Motts's theater; the first Black-owned theater in Chicago (commonly cited 1905-1911). Verify dates via primary sources before public use.

rows.name: Regal Theater (original)
rows.evidence_note: Opened 1928; white-chain controlled until S.B. Fuller purchased it in 1961; Fuller lost it in 1968; closed circa 1968 and demolished 1973 (City of Chicago landmark report; Encyclopedia of Chicago).

rows.name: New Regal Theater (Avalon)
rows.evidence_note: The 1927 Avalon Theater renovated and renamed the New Regal in 1987 by Edward and Bettiann Gardner — a geographic/name succession of the Regal concept, not the original 47th Street complex. Closed circa 2011 (commonly cited); verify exact closure year before public use.

rows.name: Sunset Cafe / Grand Terrace Cafe
rows.evidence_note: Landmark jazz venue of the Black Metropolis era (a designated Black Metropolis Chicago Landmark). Commonly cited 1921-1937; verify dates before public use.

rows.name: Checkerboard Lounge
rows.evidence_note: South Side blues club (423 E. 43rd) associated with Buddy Guy and L.C. Thurman; original building demolished 2003 and the club reopened in Hyde Park the same year (commonly cited). Relocated rather than closed.

rows.name: Knights of Pythias of North America (National Pythian Temple, Chicago)
rows.evidence_note: Temple built 1925-30 at a cost of $1M — 'the largest structure financed, designed and built by African Americans' (architect Walter T. Bailey). Financial difficulties led to WPA acquisition and reuse as multifamily housing during the Depression; vacated in the 1970s; demolished 1980 (City of Chicago Morning Star Baptist landmark report).

rows.name: Improved Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks of the World (Black Elks, Chicago lodges)
rows.evidence_note: The Black Elks (IBPOEW) continue nationally, but this track did not establish founding dates, lodge locations, or current activity for Chicago lodges — marked unknown. Flagged as a research gap.

rows.name: Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Illinois
rows.evidence_note: Prince Hall Freemasonry in Illinois commonly dated to 1867; operating. Verify founding date before public use.

rows.name: Wabash Avenue YMCA
rows.evidence_note: Black YMCA of the Great Migration era, substantially enabled by Julius Rosenwald philanthropy. Closed 1981 after declining membership and building deterioration (Wikipedia). Rehabilitated by the Renaissance Collaborative as 101 units of supportive housing plus 20,000 sq ft of recreation/office space (City of Chicago DOH, 2023). Housing function replaced in altered form; whether job-placement/training and citywide social-center functions were replaced remains unresolved.

rows.name: Ada S. McKinley Community Services (South Side Settlement)
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1919 by Ada Sophia McKinley to serve Black WWI veterans denied government services and Great Migration families; renamed for McKinley in 1949. Still operating: 70+ program sites across Chicago metro, Wisconsin, and Indiana; 2025 grant activity; CEO Jamal Malone (Cause IQ; Wikipedia; Business Wire 2024).

rows.name: Jane Addams Hull House Association
rows.evidence_note: Announced closure January 19, 2012; shut January 27, 2012; filed for bankruptcy after ~122 years, with up to 85% of revenue from public sources (Wikipedia; Chronicle of Philanthropy; NPR). The unaffiliated UIC Jane Addams Hull-House Museum remains open.

rows.name: The Renaissance Collaborative
rows.evidence_note: Community development organization; rehabilitated the Wabash Avenue YMCA. Operating status per general knowledge; confirm founding year before public use.

rows.name: Negro Fellowship League
rows.evidence_note: Opened 1910 by Ida B. Wells and Ferdinand Barnett with initial white-publisher financing; Wells later subsidized it from her probation-officer salary; closed 1920 when costs became unsustainable (TN Museum; Wikipedia). Provided lodging and job placement for Black male migrants. No successor identified — a strong no-replacement function-loss case.

rows.name: NAACP Chicago Branch
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1913. Operating.

rows.name: Chicago Urban League
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1916. Operating.

rows.name: Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters (Chicago Division)
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1925 by A. Philip Randolph; merged into the Brotherhood of Railway and Airline Clerks in 1978 (commonly cited). Verify merger details before public use.

rows.name: The Woodlawn Organization (TWO)
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1961 through local Black clergy and community leadership with organizing expertise from Saul Alinsky's Industrial Areas Foundation; later Ford/federal/corporate grants shifted it toward service provision (Domhoff article via community-wealth.org). Still active per general knowledge; confirm current activity before public use.

rows.name: Coordinating Council of Community Organizations (CCCO)
rows.evidence_note: Local coalition led by Al Raby that partnered with SCLC in the Chicago Freedom Movement; dissolved in late 1967 (Middlebury Chicago Freedom Movement site; Chicago Reporter). No direct coalition successor identified — later campaigns inherited pieces, not the coordinating structure.

rows.name: Operation Breadbasket (SCLC)
rows.evidence_note: SCLC department publicly identified with Jesse Jackson; Jackson resigned December 1971 and carried much of the program into Operation PUSH (archive.org Breadbasket history).

rows.name: Operation PUSH
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1971 by Jesse Jackson after resigning from SCLC/Breadbasket. Merged with the National Rainbow Coalition in 1996 to form the Rainbow PUSH Coalition.

rows.name: Rainbow PUSH Coalition
rows.evidence_note: Formed 1996 by merger of Operation PUSH and the National Rainbow Coalition. Operating.

rows.name: Contract Buyers League
rows.evidence_note: Organized 500+ members against contract selling; won contract renegotiations but lawsuits failed, and contract selling continued in altered form (Chicago Catholic, 2017). Active late 1960s-early 1970s; exact end date uncertain.

rows.name: Black Panther Party (Illinois Chapter)
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1968 (Fred Hampton, Bobby Rush). Commonly cited end ~1974 amid repression and internal splits; verify before public use.

rows.name: South Center Department Store
rows.evidence_note: Black-owned department store of the Black Metropolis commercial corridor; part of the Regal Theater commercial complex. Commonly cited 1929-1948; verify dates and fate (demolished with Regal complex?) before public use.

rows.name: Chicago American Giants
rows.evidence_note: Founded 1911 by Rube Foster after leaving the Leland Giants; charter members of Foster's Negro National League; most dominant team in Black baseball into the mid-1930s. Dropped from the Negro American League in 1952 and barnstormed; disbanded by the mid-1950s (sources differ: 1952 league exit vs. 1955/56 disbanding; brief 1958 revival). Exact end date disputed — do not present a single year as certain (Wikipedia; Alchetron).

rows.name: Harlem Globetrotters (founded Chicago)
rows.evidence_note: Founded in Chicago in 1926 (Savoy Ballroom) by Abe Saperstein; now headquartered in Atlanta under Herschend ownership. The institution survives but its Chicago institutional presence ended — a relocation case.

rows.name: A.R. Leak Funeral Home
rows.evidence_note: Family-owned Black funeral home; commonly cited founding 1933. Operating status per general knowledge; confirm before public use. Funeral homes are an under-researched type in this track — see notes.md.

rows.name: Cook County Bar Association
rows.evidence_note: Black lawyers' association; commonly cited founding 1914. Operating status per general knowledge; confirm before public use. Professional associations are an under-researched type — see notes.md.

rows.name: Eighth Regiment (Illinois National Guard, 'Fighting 8th')
rows.evidence_note: Origins in the 1871 Hannibal Guard; first U.S. armory built for a Black regiment (1914-15). The armory closed in the early 1960s (became South Central Gymnasium); the regiment was absorbed into the Illinois National Guard structure. Building reopened 1999 as Chicago Military Academy-Bronzeville (Wikipedia). Institutional continuity is as a Guard lineage, not a community-controlled institution.
